pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare with >, =, < on place-value meaning.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 read/write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparison and ordering of decimals to three places.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.3 — 'Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths. (a) Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form... (b) Compare two decimals to thousandths based on the meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, < symbols.'
• Operational details: Read decimals as fractions of the whole ('five and sixty-two thousandths', not 'five point zero six two') to keep place meaning audible. Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers (3×(1/10)+9×(1/100)+2×(1/1000)). Compare by aligning place value left-to-right, using equalising trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to defeat the 'longer-is-larger' error.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write five and sixty-two thousandths as a numeral.' Tier B: 'Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and justify.' Tier C: 'Write 347.392 in expanded form with unit fractions.'
bestPractices: Read decimals using place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the meaning stays audible
Build expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers (×1/10, ×1/100, ×1/1000) to bind each digit to its place
Compare left-to-right by place value, and equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to expose 'longer-is-larger' as false
Use a thousandths grid / decimal place-value chart so 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 are seen as nested tenths-of-tenths
Move fluently among numeral, words and expanded form in both directions
keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths
Thousandths grid (10×10×10 nesting) or 1000-cube partition of the unit
Number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison; trailing-zero alignment tool
commonMisconceptions: 'Longer decimal is larger' (0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits)
'Shorter decimal is larger' (over-correcting to 'fewer digits = closer to whole')
Reading 0.062 as 'point zero sixty-two' and losing the thousandths meaning
Treating the decimal part as a whole number after the point (comparing 372 vs 38)
Misplacing digits in expanded form — attaching 1/10 to the hundredths digit

learn.summary: Learners aged 10–11 read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, and compare with >, =, < based on place-value meaning. The central hurdle is the 'longer-is-larger' error (judging 0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits). Guidance centres on place-value alignment, equalising with trailing zeros, naming decimals by their place ('sixty-two thousandths') to keep place meaning audible, and building expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers.

activities.title: Align and compare on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner picks 0.372 as larger because '372 > 38', line the decimals up tenths-under-tenths and compare the tenths first (3 vs 3, equal), then the hundredths (7 vs 8), so 0.372 < 0.38. Padding to 0.380 shows equal-length strings so the digit-count argument disappears.
If the grid shading surprises them — the 'shorter' 0.38 shades MORE squares than the 'longer' 0.372 — ask them to restate why: 0.380 > 0.372 because the deciding place (hundredths) has 8 > 7.
Reinforce by naming the deciding place aloud: 'they are equal in the tenths, so the hundredths decides.'
activities.rationale: Comparison to thousandths depends on place-value alignment. Aligning columns, padding trailing zeros and identifying the first differing place makes the >,=,< decision follow from meaning rather than memorised rules, and directly targets the 'longer-is-larger' misconception. A grid and a number line give two further views of the same magnitude relationship.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Write two decimals into aligned Ones . tenths . hundredths . thousandths rows, e.g. 0.372 and 0.38.
Pad the shorter decimal with a trailing zero so both have the same length: 0.38 becomes 0.380.
Compare left-to-right, place by place: tenths match (3 = 3), then at the hundredths the 7 and 8 differ, so 0.372 < 0.380.
State the comparison with the correct symbol and say which place decided it.
Shade each value on a thousandths grid (380 squares vs 372 squares) and check which covers more area.
Optionally, mark both decimals on a number line to hundredths/thousandths to see their relative positions as a second representation of the same comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: The length of a decimal does not determine its size; comparison is decided by the first place where the digits differ, read left-to-right. Trailing zeros make equal-length strings without changing value (0.38 = 0.380).

activities.title: Write spoken decimals keeping placeholder zeros
feedback: If a learner writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths', ask which place the word 'thousandths' names (the third place). The 2 must sit there, so 62 becomes 062: 5.062.
Check the reverse: ask them to read 5.62 and 5.062 aloud and notice these are different numbers (sixty-two hundredths vs sixty-two thousandths).
activities.rationale: Reading digit-by-digit ('point zero six two') hides place meaning. Naming the place of the final digit forces correct placement and surfaces the need for placeholder zeros, addressing the dropped-zero error.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Read a decimal aloud using place-value names: 'five and sixty-two thousandths' rather than 'five point zero six two'.
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as a numeral, anchoring the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third decimal place.
Fill the places: 062 occupies tenths–hundredths–thousandths, giving 5.062.
Explain where the placeholder 0 goes and why it cannot be dropped.
Translate in both directions: given 5.062, say the words; given the words, write the numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a decimal by its place ('thousandths') tells you which column the last digit must occupy; a placeholder zero may be needed so the digits land in the correct places. 5.062 ≠ 5.62.

activities.title: Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers
feedback: If a learner writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths digit, extend the ×10-to-the-left / ÷10-to-the-right pattern through the point: the place right of ones is 1/10, so the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10.
If a digit is attached to the wrong unit fraction (e.g. 1/10 given to the hundredths digit), re-read the chart left-to-right naming each place in turn.
activities.rationale: Expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers binds each digit to its place and prevents expanding decimal digits with whole-number multipliers. A static labelled number with revealed place values is a useful anchor but does not itself perform the comparison alignment, so pair it with the comparison activity.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Tap or point to each digit of a number such as 347.392 and name its place and value.
Write the expanded form binding each digit to its place: 3×100 + 4×10 + 7×1 + 3×(1/10) + 9×(1/100) + 2×(1/1000).
Say what each digit is worth, e.g. 'the 9 is worth 9 hundredths, 9×(1/100)'.
Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the decimal point: each place is one tenth of the place to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
Check a tricky case: the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10, NOT by 10 or 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Expanded form makes each digit's value explicit. Decimal places continue the base-ten pattern to the right with unit-fraction multipliers (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000), one tenth of the place to the left.

activities.title: Argue and justify a comparison (discussion)
feedback: If the learner argues from digit count, redirect to the tenths-under-tenths alignment and ask which place first differs.
Accept a correct answer only with a place-value justification, not just the right symbol.
activities.rationale: A discussion that baits and corrects the 'longer-is-larger' error can usefully surface a learner's reasoning, though learners should still manipulate aligned place values to resolve the comparison. Treat talk as a complement to the alignment work, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38, and prove it?'
Make a claim and justify it by aligning place values, not by counting digits.
Defend the claim against the 'longer-is-larger' bait by padding to 0.380 and comparing the hundredths.
Put the comparison into a sentence: '0.38 is bigger because they are equal in the tenths but 8 hundredths beats 7 hundredths.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain a comparison in words — citing the first differing place — demonstrates place-value understanding rather than rule-following.

activities.title: Check and order several decimals
feedback: For a comparison item, mark a digit-count answer wrong and prompt a place-value re-check with padded zeros.
For the ordering item, have the learner write all values to the same number of places first (0.300, 0.290, 0.305, 0.310), then order the aligned strings.
For the fill-in item, confirm the placeholder zero lands in the tenths place (5.062, not 5.62).
activities.rationale: Comparing, writing from words and ordering mixed-length decimals checks the key skills and misconceptions. This verifies understanding built through manipulation and discussion; it does not by itself build the alignment intuition.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and choose >, = or <, rejecting any answer based purely on digit count.
Complete 'five and sixty-two thousandths = ___' with the correct numeral (5.062).
Order four decimals of unequal length (e.g. 0.3, 0.29, 0.305, 0.31) by padding to equal length and comparing left-to-right, giving 0.29 < 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.31.
Explain each placement rather than only giving the final order.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing and comparing decimals can be verified across numeral and word forms and by ordering, including deliberately mixed-length cases that expose the 'longer-is-larger' trap.

constraints: Read decimals with place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the place meaning stays audible.
Equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) when comparing; this exposes 'longer-is-larger' as false without changing value.
Watch for over-correction to 'shorter-is-larger' (fewer digits = closer to the whole); length alone decides nothing — only the first differing place does.
5.062 is not 5.62: keep placeholder zeros when a spoken place name requires the final digit to sit further right.

A static labelled number with revealed place values anchors reading and expanded form but cannot carry out the padding/alignment that resolves comparisons; use it alongside the comparison activity, not instead of it.
Recognition or multiple-choice checks verify the skill but do not require the learner to construct alignment reasoning independently; include tasks where they write and justify.

Grid shading, column-highlight tools and a number line to hundredths/thousandths are illustrative, complementary supports for the comparison mechanism, not required equipment; the reasoning can also be carried out on paper by writing values to equal length.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row's 'quiz' companion and 'conversation' options were retained as the check/ordering activity and the discussion activity respectively, with product and fit-ranking vocabulary removed.
The source keyRepresentations listed a 'number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison'; it is reinstated as an optional comparison representation in Activity 1 and the constraints.

The source claimed decimal notation is 'planar and symbolic' so '3D adds no explanatory power' for this topic; this is a reasonable scoping judgement for comparison/notation but is not an established universal law, so it is not asserted as one here.

The original framing that an interactive comparator uniquely makes comparison 'felt, not memorised' is softened: alignment, grid and trailing-zero reasoning can also be done on paper; the interactive example is one concrete medium.
The second CCSS-M source is marked unverified in the row (verified:false); its claim is retained as stated but not treated as independently confirmed.
Activity 5's insight was narrowed to the forms it actually tests (numeral/word forms and ordering); expanded-form checking remains in Activity 3.

probeDeeper: Line up 0.372 and 0.38 by place — which is bigger and why?
Write sixty-two thousandths on its own — where does the 0 go?

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Longer decimal is larger': says 0.372 > 0.38 because 372 > 38 / it has more digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align by place (tenths under tenths); compare tenths first (3 vs 8). Pad with a zero (0.380) to see equal-length strings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The decimal with more digits is chosen regardless of place value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero in a spoken decimal: writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third place, so 062 fills tenths–hundredths–thousandths → 5.062.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sixty-two thousandths is placed in the tenths/hundredths instead of hundredths/thousandths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expanded form mishandles the fractional places: writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths instead of 3×(1/10)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the point: each place is 1/10 of the one to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Decimal digits are expanded with whole-number multipliers.

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'longer-is-larger', drops placeholder zeros, or expands decimals with whole-number multipliers.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes (numerals/words/expanded) and compares decimals to thousandths by place value, keeping placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Reads/writes tidy decimals but slips on comparisons of unequal length or on spoken thousandths.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch across forms. 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38? Line them up to decide. Write “five and sixty-two thousandths” as a decimal. Then write 347.392 in expanded form.' Watch the comparison reasoning and the placeholder zero in the thousandths write.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 0.372 vs 0.38 is the classic 'longer-is-larger' trap — a child comparing digit-strings picks 0.372. 'Sixty-two thousandths' needs a placeholder zero in the tenths (5.062), catching the child who writes 5.62. Expanded form checks each decimal place carries its unit fraction.
